FAQ

Questions anglers ask.

Is TroutScout free?

Yes. Fish Scores, maps, today's conditions, hatch charts, the community and your catch log are free. Premium ($7.99/month or $34.99/year, with a 3-day free trial on the yearly plan) unlocks stocking details, alerts for all your streams, the full forecast and more.

Where does the Fish Score come from?

It's built from live NOAA weather and rainfall, USGS stream gauges, the time of day and season, recent stockings, hatches in season and today's angler reports. It's a guide to the best times, not a guarantee.

Which states are covered?

All 50 U.S. states have Fish Scores. Stocking, native trout and regulation coverage depends on what each state's wildlife agency publishes; Pennsylvania has the deepest data.

Will other anglers see my fishing spots?

No. Your catch log is private. You choose what to share, and you can share a catch without its location.

Does it work on Android?

TroutScout is on iPhone first. Follow @troutscoutapp for news.

Map guide

Every trout layer, explained.

Turn on any layer in the map's Layers menu. Here's what each one means, with a real example.

Stocked Waters

Streams and lakes the state stocks with hatchery-raised trout, from the state stocking reports. Tap a stream to see when it was last stocked and with which species.

Example A local creek that gets rainbow and brown trout every spring before opening day.

Stocking Sections

The exact stretch of a stream where the state releases trout, traced from the stocking list's upper and lower limits - not the whole stream. Pennsylvania only.

Example A creek listed as stocked "from the Route 45 bridge downstream to the mouth" is drawn only along that stretch.

Wild Trout Waters

Streams where trout reproduce naturally - the fish were born in the stream, not raised in a hatchery. The species can be native or one introduced long ago.

Example A mountain creek full of wild brown trout (originally from Europe) is a wild trout water even though browns are not native.

Premier Wild Trout Waters

The best wild trout water in each state - the state's own top classification, based on how many wild trout the stream holds. Each stream keeps the state's name for its class.

Example Pennsylvania's Class A Wild Trout Streams or Wisconsin's Class I Trout Waters.

Designated Trout Waters

Waters a state officially lists as trout water, often with special rules (catch and release, fly fishing only, delayed harvest). Includes wild, stocked and trophy waters.

Example Colorado's Gold Medal Waters, Montana's Blue Ribbon streams, or a state's official trout stream list.

Native Trout Regions

Shaded areas on the map where a trout species that has always lived in that region still survives - fish that were there long before any stocking. These are often remote headwaters inside state forests, wilderness areas and national forests.

Example Brook trout in Pennsylvania's state forests or the Great Smoky Mountains; cutthroat trout in Colorado; Apache trout in Arizona.

Stream Gauges

Live USGS gauges on the map. Tap one for current flow and gauge height, with a chart of the last few days, so you know if the water is high, low or just right.

Example Flow jumps after a storm - check the gauge before you drive.

Wild vs native trout

WildNative
How fish get thereBorn in the wild (stream-bred)Born in the wild (stream-bred)
Where species came fromCan be native OR non-native (e.g., wild brown trout)Must be historically indigenous to the region (e.g., native brook trout)
Management focusSupporting natural reproduction and self-sustaining sport fisheriesPreserving original regional genetics and pristine habitats
